analysis.one_liner: Requires electric utilities to get 8-50% of electricity from renewables or efficiency by 2040.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2012 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require large electric utilities to obtain an increasing share of the electricity they sell from renewable sources like wind, solar, and hydropower or from proven efficiency savings, rising from 8% in 2014 to 50% by 2035. Utilities could meet up to a quarter of the target with efficiency savings (up to half if a governor asks), or pay $50 per shortfall into state funds for clean energy and efficiency programs. Utilities that missed their targets would owe double penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers would benefit if efficiency investments lower electricity demand and long-term fuel and pollution costs fall; renewable energy manufacturers, installers, and efficiency service companies would gain a guaranteed national market as utilities buy credits to meet the standard.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, renewable energy and efficiency industries

how_it_helps.text: Sets a national standard requiring large electric utilities to source an increasing share of electricity from renewables or efficiency savings, reaching 50% by 2035 [S3] [S2].
Requires states to spend alternative compliance payments from utilities on renewable energy deployment or cost-effective efficiency programs [S3] [S2].
Imposes civil penalties on utilities that fail to meet their targets, giving the requirement teeth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electric utilities and their shareholders would bear the cost of building or buying renewable energy and efficiency programs; costs could pass through to ratepayers depending on state regulation.

drawbacks.text: The $50 per-megawatt-hour alternative compliance payment could prove cheaper than building new renewable capacity in some regions, letting utilities pay rather than transition [S3].
Compliance costs would likely flow through state-regulated electricity rates, raising bills for consumers in areas lacking cheap renewables [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would speed the shift off fossil electricity and cut long-run pollution and fuel costs, but would raise utility compliance costs that could partly pass through to ratepayers, and the $50 buyout and credit trading create loopholes that could dilute the standard's effect.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2012 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee, no further action taken [S5].
Congress ended January 3, 2013 without the bill advancing [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel generators and utilities invested in existing power plants benefited because no new renewable procurement requirements were imposed; renewable energy industries lost a potential guaranteed market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent fossil generators and their suppliers

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed for a federal renewable electricity and efficiency standard.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the only support shown was two Democratic cosponsors, with no committee action either way.

industries.note: Would gain a large guaranteed national market as utilities bought renewable credits to meet the standard.
Would face pressure as utilities shifted procurement away from fossil sources toward renewables.

industries.industry: Energy service companies and efficiency contractors
industries.note: Would profit from utilities contracting with third-party efficiency providers to meet savings targets.
